value.overview: The Scarlet-rumped Cacique is a striking black cacique of humid tropical forests in Central and South America. Its most distinctive feature is the bright scarlet patch on the lower back and rump, which may be hidden when the bird is perched. It belongs to the New World blackbird family and is usually seen in the forest canopy, where it searches for insects, fruit, nectar, and other small food items. In Costa Rica, it is primarily a resident of the Caribbean lowlands.
value.classification: The species is a passerine in the family Icteridae. The Costa Rican and other Central American birds have traditionally been treated as the subspecies Cacicus uropygialis microrhynchus, but many modern taxonomies recognize this population as the separate Scarlet-rumped Cacique, Cacicus microrhynchus, while reserving C. uropygialis for the Subtropical Cacique of the Andes.
value.identification: A medium-sized, slender cacique with mostly glossy black plumage, a long pointed pale ivory bill, and pale bluish or whitish eyes. A vivid scarlet patch covers the rump and lower back, although it is often difficult to see from below or when the wings are folded. The sexes are similar in color, but males are generally larger. Its varied song includes clear whistles and ringing notes, while calls may be short, sharp, or nasal.
value.rangeHabitat: The Central American form occurs from eastern Honduras through Nicaragua, Costa Rica, and Panama, with related populations extending into northwestern South America. In Costa Rica, it is mainly a resident of the humid Caribbean lowlands and foothills, including areas around Sarapiquí and La Selva; it also occurs locally in other wet forest regions. It uses mature and secondary evergreen forest, forest edges, clearings with tall trees, plantations, and other wooded habitats, generally where dense vegetation and a well-developed canopy remain.
value.migrationStatus: Resident in Costa Rica. It is not considered a regular long-distance migrant, although local movements may occur in response to food availability, breeding, or seasonal conditions.
value.breeding: The species builds a long, hanging, pouch-like nest from plant fibers, usually suspended from an outer branch high above the ground. The female generally lays about two eggs, and she performs most or all incubation while both adults help feed the young. In Costa Rica, breeding has been recorded in lowland forest and wooded habitats. Pairs commonly nest alone, although small groups or loose colonies may occur in some areas.
value.dietFeeding: Its diet includes large insects, spiders, other arthropods, fruit, berries, nectar, and occasionally small vertebrates. It usually feeds in the middle and upper canopy, moving deliberately among foliage and branches. Individuals may join mixed-species feeding flocks or travel in small family groups. The long, pointed bill is useful for probing flowers, extracting insect prey, and handling soft fruits.
value.behavior: Scarlet-rumped Caciques are active, vocal canopy birds that are often detected by sound before they are seen. They may occur singly, in pairs, or in small groups and sometimes associate with mixed feeding flocks. Their movements through the canopy can be quick and purposeful, with frequent pauses to call or inspect foliage. The bright rump is most conspicuous during flight or when the bird stretches, turns, or raises its wings.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population trend is not reliably quantified in the available sources, but the species is not currently considered globally threatened.
